extracted.intended_audience: general public and science-interested readers (also useful to researchers interested in reproducibility)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for assessing whether experimental cancer biology results can be reproduced across labs, and for designing transparent replication efforts. Focuses on issues such as transparency, methods detail, material sharing, resources, and interpretation of differing results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility as a central evaluative feature
rubrics_metrics.description: “Reproducibility is a central feature of how science is supposed to be, and it's not clear to what extent it is happening in practice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether independent labs can repeat experiments and obtain the same results is a core quality criterion; failures to reproduce raise concerns about the reliability of findings (example: Bayer and Amgen's widely reported failed attempts to redo dozens of promising cancer experiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about study selection, methods, and study plans
rubrics_metrics.description: The reproducibility project was “transparent about how it picked the studies, transparent about their methods and their study plans.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openly documenting selection criteria, protocols, and pre-specified study plans enables others to follow up and evaluate replication work; lack of disclosure (as with Bayer and Amgen not revealing which experiments they examined) hampers community assessment and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original-lab cooperation and sharing of materials/protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples where original labs cooperated by providing materials: “the lab gave us the same drug... they gave us the same tumor cells that they used.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation (sharing drugs, cell lines, detailed protocols) can reduce sources of error and help replication, but sharing materials does not guarantee replication success — replicated labs may still obtain different results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and clarity of published directions/methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Question posed: “Are the directions offered in a paper too sketchy? Or maybe an experiment only works under certain unusual conditions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should check whether methods sections provide sufficient detail for replication; vague/sketchy instructions or omission of critical conditions are anti-patterns that impede reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate time and resources for replication attempts
rubrics_metrics.description: “One of the difficulties of the reproducibility project is that they have limited time and resources to spend on any one study... they can't go back and do these things over and over again when the first attempts turn out to be uninterpretable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replication projects should budget sufficient time and funding because many experiments require months/years to perfect techniques; under-resourced replications may yield uninterpretable or premature conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness across multiple attempts / need for repeated optimization
rubrics_metrics.description: “It can take months or years to perfect the laboratory techniques used in any given experiment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single failed replication may not prove the original result false; robustness should be assessed across multiple, well-conducted attempts and optimization of techniques when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful interpretation of discrepant replication results
rubrics_metrics.description: “The inevitable question then is whether the original science was wrong or whether the scientists who tried to repeat that work tripped up.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When replication differs from original findings, evaluators should consider multiple explanations (experimental error, subtle differences in conditions, original result issues) rather than immediately attributing blame to either side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic meta-research to identify common causes of non-reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “They're looking for patterns across cancer research and also trying to identify common reasons that labs might have trouble reproducing one another's work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond individual replications, projects should aggregate results across many studies to discover recurring causes (e.g., methodological vagueness, context-specific effects) and inform best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open, collaborative project design (pre-registration and coordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nosek’s reproducibility project emphasized being open about selection and methods and worked “in collaboration with a company called Science Exchange.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-registered replication plans, collaborative platforms, and open communication between original and replicating labs are recommended design features to increase credibility and allow community scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical/translational relevance as a motivator for replication
rubrics_metrics.description: “The conversation is important because the vast majority of treatment ideas that come from this basic science fail when they're tried in people... scientists often don't know why those failures occur.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproducibility should be evaluated with an eye to downstream clinical implications: unreproducible basic findings can misdirect investments in drug development and patient care, so replication has high practical stakes.
